market_context: United States/international; opened cooked deli meats, sliced cold cuts, and dry-cured meats in household refrigeration.
title: How Long Do Opened Deli Meats Last in the Refrigerator?

seo.title: How Long Do Opened Deli Meats Last in the Fridge?
seo.meta_description: Opened cooked lunch meat and deli-sliced meat generally keep 3–5 days refrigerated. Dry-cured salami, prosciutto, or similar meats can have much longer product-specific windows. Follow the label and identify the type of meat before applying a storage rule.
seo.search_intent: Understand how long opened deli meats keep, why cooked cold cuts differ from dry-cured meats, and which storage and spoilage signs matter.

excerpt: There is no single refrigerator window for every food called a deli meat or cold cut. For moist cooked lunch meats—ham, turkey, bologna, and similar sliced products—USDA uses 3–5 days after opening or deli slicing. Dry-cured salami, prosciutto, and similar products can have very different storage lives. Processing method and package directions matter more than applying one rule to all cured meats.
content_html:
For opened cooked lunch meat or deli-sliced cold cuts, 3–5 refrigerated days at 40 °F (4 °C) or below is the standard U.S. reference. This fits products such as sliced cooked ham, turkey, bologna, and many sandwich meats.

But “deli meat” can also include dry-cured products. Dry salami, prosciutto, and cooked turkey are not microbiologically or physically the same food.

Opened moist lunch meats generally get 3–5 days

FoodSafety.gov and USDA list 3–5 days for luncheon meat after a package is opened or when meat has been sliced at the deli counter.

These products are moist, ready to eat, and exposed to handling after processing. Opening also removes the protection of the original sealed environment.

If the package says “use within three days of opening,” follow that shorter instruction.

Dry-cured meats are a different category

Dry salami, cured chorizo, prosciutto, and selected hams lose water during curing and may use salt, fermentation, and other hurdles that slow microbial growth.

Some therefore keep for weeks or longer under specific conditions. USDA, for example, gives sliced prosciutto, Parma, or Serrano-style ham a much longer refrigerated window than ordinary cooked lunch meat.

Do not transfer that long window to a fresh or cooked sausage simply because both products are called sausage.

Factory packaging and deli slicing differ too

A factory-sealed pack may use modified atmosphere and tightly controlled filling. Deli slicing introduces cutting surfaces and extra handling.

This is why the same 3–5 day reference applies to many meats sliced at the store even when they were purchased that day.

Store slices tightly covered and do not return pieces that have sat on a serving plate for a long time to the main package.

Listeria is one reason storage time matters

Ready-to-eat deli meats can occasionally become contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes after cooking. Unlike many foodborne bacteria, Listeria can grow slowly at refrigerator temperatures.

Keeping the refrigerator cold and limiting storage time is particularly important for pregnant people, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems.

Public-health agencies may recommend reheating selected deli meats until steaming for higher-risk individuals.

What spoilage signs matter?

New slime, sour or rancid odor, unexpected mold, gas, package swelling, or abnormal color are reasons to discard a product.

Selected dry-cured meats can have an intentional surface culture, so know what is normal for that specific product.

Pathogens do not always create a bad smell, so sensory checks cannot replace refrigerator time and temperature.

How to store opened deli meat

Keep it at 40 °F or below in a tightly closed package or container. Use clean hands or utensils when separating slices.

Many lunch meats can be frozen, with USDA using roughly 1–2 months as a best-quality window. Thawed slices may lose some moisture or texture.

Freeze portions while they are still fresh rather than after they have already exceeded the refrigerator window.

Use the right rule for the right product

First identify whether the meat is moist and cooked, dry cured, fresh, or fermented. Then check the manufacturer's after-opening direction.

For ordinary cooked or deli-sliced lunch meat without a different instruction, 3–5 days is a useful benchmark. For dry-cured meat, use product-specific guidance.

The practical rule: do not apply “one week” to every cold cut. Think 3–5 days for opened moist lunch meat; for dry-cured products, identify the product and follow its specific label because storage can be much longer.

faq.question: How long does opened sliced ham last?
faq.answer: For ordinary cooked deli ham, a standard refrigerator reference is 3–5 days at 40°F or below.

faq.question: Does dry salami only last 3–5 days?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Dry-cured meats can have substantially longer storage windows depending on processing, moisture, format, and label instructions.

faq.question: How long does meat sliced at the deli counter last?
faq.answer: USDA uses 3–5 days for luncheon meat that is opened or deli sliced.
